newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus surges, fuels trade tension jitters.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus surges, fuels trade tension jitters.

text.p: The surplus in Japan's politically sensitive current account surged by more than 90 percent in April as higher taxes dampened imports and the strong U.S. economy sucked in Japanese goods, the government said on Wednesday.

The dramatic rise in the surplus, which threatened to inflame tensions with key trading partners such as the United States, sent only gentle ripples through financial markets, which had been expecting the trade gap to widen sharply.

But swift comments from U.S. Deputy Treasury Lawrence Summers warning Japan to avoid running up external surpluses sent the dollar spiralling down through 111 yen to 110.97 yen, its lowest level in almost seven months.

The surplus in the current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose 92.7 percent to 1.09 trillion yen ($9.8 billion) in April from a year earlier, while the surplus in merchandise trade alone rose 90.9 percent to 1.02 trillion yen ($9.1 billion), the Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) said.

"We had a consumption tax hike the same month which dramatically depressed import growth, which is one of the major reasons behind the growth in the trade surplus," Andrew Shipley, economist at Schroders Japan Ltd told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV), adding that strong U.S. economy was also helping Japanese exports.
Japan raised its consumption tax from three to five percent on April 1.
The dollar rose as high as around 112.70 yen after the release of the trade data, which was within analysts' expectations, after standing at around 112.19 yen in late New York trading on Tuesday.

But it soon fell back and selling gathered pace after Summers said in a speech prepared for delivery to a trade group in Denver that Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth and should foster demand-led recovery at home.
The trade data had only muted impact on Tokyo stocks as the surge in the surplus was expected.

"A more than one trillion yen ($9.0 billion) surplus for trade and the current account was expected by most observers. Actually, it was not a big surprise," said Masanobu Takahashi, director and head of research at Sanyo Investment Research.

Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Baring Securities, said: "People are interested not so much in the April numbers but in the May figures for customs-cleared trade, which will show the surplus more than doubled. So these figures are not a one-off fluke, it's the beginning of a trend of a strongly rising surplus."
The Ministry of Finance said the surplus was unlikely to rise significantly in the medium to longer term.

Shipley said a downward trend in the surplus should resume in due course. "We see the current account surplus resuming its long-term trend downwards from the second half of the year on the back of slowing overseas demand and resumption of economic growth following fiscal tightening," he said.
Although there are concerns in the markets about looming trade friction with the United States, Sanyo's Takahashi said that there was too much anxiety over the issue.

The issue is expected to come up at the Group of Seven (G7) summit of industrialised nations in Denver later this month. But U.S. President Bill Clinton is not expected to be as forceful on the subject as he was when he met Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in April, G7 officials in Washington said.
